```{python}
#| label: setup
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.optimize import linprog
from _lib.orplot import COLORS
```

## The idea

A linear program has three parts:

1. **Decision variables**: the numbers you get to choose.
2. **An objective**: a linear function of them, to maximize or minimize.
3. **Constraints**: linear equations or inequalities they must satisfy.

"Linear" means every term is a constant times a single variable: no products of
variables, no powers, no "if" statements. That restriction is what makes LPs so
tractable.

**Example (the workshop).** A workshop makes chairs and tables. A chair uses 1 unit of
wood and 2 hours of labor and earns a profit of 3; a table uses 2 units of wood and 1 hour
of labor and earns 4. This week there are 8 units of wood and 7 hours of labor. With
$x_1$ chairs and $x_2$ tables:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\max\quad & 3x_1 + 4x_2 && \text{(profit)}\\
\text{s.t.}\quad & x_1 + 2x_2 \le 8 && \text{(wood)}\\
& 2x_1 + x_2 \le 7 && \text{(labor)}\\
& x_1, x_2 \ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
$$
Every constraint reads the same way: *resource used* $\le$ *resource available*. Each
column is one activity (a product), and each row is one resource. This "activities and
resources" reading is how most LPs are built.

## A bit of history

Linear programming was found twice. In 1939 Leonid Kantorovich formulated production
planning problems of exactly this kind and proposed a way to solve them; his work became
widely known in the West only with its 1960 translation [@kantorovich1960]. In 1947
George Dantzig formulated the general LP for US Air Force planning and invented the
simplex method to solve it [@dantzig1951]. Meanwhile @stigler1945 posed the famous **diet
problem**: find the cheapest combination of foods that meets given nutritional
requirements. He could only solve it approximately by hand, because no general method was
available yet.

## The math

### General form

In matrix notation, an LP is
$$
\max\ c^\top x \quad \text{s.t.} \quad Ax \le b, \quad x \ge 0 ,
$$
with $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ the objective coefficients, $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ the
technology matrix (resource $i$ used per unit of activity $j$), and $b \in \mathbb{R}^m$
the right-hand side (resource availabilities). In the workshop,
$A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\ 2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, $b = (8, 7)$, $c = (3, 4)$.

### Every LP can be put in any standard form

Different books and solvers use different "standard forms." They are all equivalent,
because each feature can be converted into any other:

| You have | Rewrite it as |
|---|---|
| $\min\ c^\top x$ | $\max\ -c^\top x$ |
| $a^\top x \ge \beta$ | $-a^\top x \le -\beta$ |
| $a^\top x = \beta$ | $a^\top x \le \beta$ and $a^\top x \ge \beta$ |
| $a^\top x \le \beta$ | $a^\top x + s = \beta$ with a **slack** variable $s \ge 0$ |
| a free variable $x_j$ (any sign) | $x_j = x_j^+ - x_j^-$ with $x_j^+, x_j^- \ge 0$ |

The slack form $Ax + s = b$, $x, s \ge 0$ is the one the simplex method works with. In
the workshop, the slacks $s_1, s_2$ are the leftover wood and labor.

### Modeling tricks: what LPs can and cannot express

Some nonlinear-looking things are LPs in disguise. The common thread is
[convexity](../../foundations/convexity/convex-functions.qmd).

- **Maximum of linear functions.** To minimize $\max_k (a_k^\top x + \beta_k)$, add a
  variable $t$, minimize $t$, and require $t \ge a_k^\top x + \beta_k$ for every $k$.
- **Absolute values.** To minimize $\sum_i |r_i|$ where each $r_i$ is linear in $x$, add
  $u_i$ with $u_i \ge r_i$ and $u_i \ge -r_i$, and minimize $\sum_i u_i$.
- **Piecewise-linear convex costs** (for example, overtime that costs more per hour) are
  a maximum of linear functions, so the first trick applies.

Things an LP cannot express:

- **Products of variables**, such as price $\times$ quantity when both are decisions.
- **Either–or and on/off logic**, such as "a machine is either off or produces at least
  10 units." That needs binary variables: see
  [Disjunctive Programming](../../integer-programming/disjunctive-programming/introduction.qmd).
- **Integrality**, such as "whole tables only." For the workshop the optimum happens to be
  integer; in general it is not, and that is
  [Integer Programming](../../integer-programming/index.qmd).

### An example of the absolute-value trick: robust line fitting

Fitting a line $y \approx \alpha + \beta t$ to data by minimizing the **sum of absolute
errors** $\sum_i |y_i - \alpha - \beta t_i|$ is an LP by the trick above. Unlike least
squares, it is barely moved by a single bad data point.

```{python}
#| label: fig-l1-fit
#| fig-cap: "Fitting a line to 12 points, one of which (red) is a gross outlier. The fit minimizing the sum of absolute errors (blue) is computed by an LP and passes through the bulk of the data. The least-squares fit (dashed grey) is pulled toward the outlier, because squaring makes one large error count heavily."
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
t = np.linspace(0, 10, 12)
y = 1.0 + 0.6 * t + rng.normal(0, 0.35, t.size)
y[9] += 6.0                                     # one outlier
n = t.size
# variables: alpha, beta, u_1..u_n ; minimize sum u
cost = np.r_[0, 0, np.ones(n)]
X = np.c_[np.ones(n), t]
A_ub = np.block([[-X, -np.eye(n)], [X, -np.eye(n)]])   # u >= y - Xw and u >= Xw - y
b_ub = np.r_[-y, y]
res = linprog(cost, A_ub=A_ub, b_ub=b_ub,
              bounds=[(None, None)] * 2 + [(0, None)] * n, method="highs")
a1, b1 = res.x[:2]
a2, b2 = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 3.6))
ok = np.arange(n) != 9
ax.scatter(t[ok], y[ok], color="black", s=22, zorder=3)
ax.scatter(t[9], y[9], color=COLORS["weak"], s=40, zorder=3, label="outlier")
tt = np.linspace(-0.3, 10.3, 2)
ax.plot(tt, a1 + b1 * tt, color=COLORS["p1"], lw=2.2, label="sum of |errors| (an LP)")
ax.plot(tt, a2 + b2 * tt, color="gray", lw=1.6, ls="--", label="least squares")
ax.set_xlabel("$t$"); ax.set_ylabel("$y$")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=9)
plt.show()
```

## In practice

- **Write the model in words first**: "for each product, for each resource, ...".
  Index sets and sums come from those sentences.
- **Check units.** Every term in a constraint must have the same units (hours, kilograms,
  dollars).
- **Modeling languages** (AMPL, JuMP, Pyomo, PuLP and others) let you write the
  algebraic model directly; the solver never sees anything but $A$, $b$, $c$.
- **Size is rarely the problem.** LPs with millions of variables are solved routinely.
  Getting the model right is usually the hard part.
